title: Esters
learningObjective: know that esters contain the functional group; know that ethyl ethanoate is the ester produced when ethanol and ethanoic acid react in the presence of an acid catalyst; understand how to write the structural and displayed formulae of ethyl ethanoate; understand how to write the structural and displayed formulae of an ester, given the name or formula of the alcohol and carboxylic acid from which it is formed and vice versa; know that esters are volatile compounds with distinctive smells and are used as food flavourings and in perfumes; practical: prepare a sample of an ester such as ethyl ethanoate

sections.title: Esters
sections.markdown:
**Alcohols, carboxylic acids and esters** are organic
compounds that contain oxygen as well as carbon and hydrogen —
and they are closely related. The [[alcohol]]s carry –OH, and
oxidising them builds the [[carboxylic-acid]]s with their –COOH
group (u4:c26, u4:c27). This lesson adds the third member of
that oxygen-bearing trio. An
[[ester]] forms when an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid —
the –OH-bearing families join, water is expelled, and the
product is neither an alcohol nor an acid but something new.
That new family runs the flavour and perfume industry: esters
are frequently used for perfumes and artificial flavourings,
and you will meet them every time fruit scent appears in a
chemistry question.

Every family member carries the same [[functional-group]]: two
oxygen atoms arranged around one carbon, written in condensed
form as **–COO–**. Read the arrangement bond by bond:

```
      O
      ‖
—C—O—
```

The carbon at the centre carries a double bond to one oxygen
(C=O) and a single bond to the other (C–O), and it sits in the
chain with one bond spare on each side — that is what lets it
bridge the acid fragment and the alcohol fragment. The –COO–
group is the ester's signature the way –OH is the alcohol's and
–COOH is the acid's: spot it in a formula and you have found an
ester.

The family is not a laboratory curiosity. Olive oil,
sunflower oil, butter and cream are all built from natural
esters: their fat and oil molecules carry the same –COO–
arrangement, which is why this family's chemistry reaches from
a test tube to the kitchen. The small esters are the ones with
the famous smells, and their volatility makes those smells
travel — a property the uses section turns into chemistry
(4.42C). First, though, the group itself: everything else in
this lesson is drawn from it.

:::prior-knowledge
Three ideas load this lesson. First, the alcohol family and its
–OH group, including the two oxidation routes that build
carboxylic acids from them (u4:c26). Second, the carboxylic-acid
family with its –COOH group and its naming habit of counting all
carbons including the acid carbon (u4:c27). Third, the position
of equilibrium and how it responds to changes you make (u3:c21)
— esterification is reversible, so that idea decides the yield.
If any of those wobble, repair them before the making section,
because the reaction there uses all three.
:::

:::exam-hint
Statement 4.38C says *know* that esters contain the functional
group — a recall item. Reproduce –COO– from memory: a carbon
with C=O to one oxygen and C–O to the other. The classic lost
mark is writing –COOH (that is the carboxylic-acid group, with
its hydrogen still attached) or –CO– (one oxygen only). Two
oxygens, one carbon, no hydrogen on the group: that is –COO–.
:::

:::misconception
"–COO– and –COOH are the same group written differently." They
are different families. The ester group has no hydrogen on its
second oxygen — the acid's hydrogen is exactly what leaves when
the ester forms. Writing the acid's –COOH where an ester's
–COO– belongs changes the compound: the hydrogen is not
decoration, it is the difference between a family that donates
protons and one that smells of pear.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you draw the ester functional group with the C=O and C–O
bonds both explicit, and write its condensed form? Can you say
which two families react to make an ester? Can you name three
everyday materials built from natural esters? If yes, the
–COO– signature is loaded and the making section is next.
:::

sections.title: Making a simple ester: ethyl ethanoate
sections.markdown:
Heat a mixture of ethanoic acid and ethanol with a few drops of
concentrated sulfuric acid and a new colourless liquid appears:
**[[ethyl-ethanoate]]**, the ester of this lesson (4.39C). The
equation of record carries every atom, with the word labels
under each formula:

CH₃COOH(l) + CH₃CH₂OH(l) → CH₃COOCH₂CH₃(l) + H₂O(l)

ethanoic acid + ethanol → ethyl ethanoate + water

Three practical details sit under that equation, and the
examiners ask for all of them. The **starting materials** are
ethanol and ethanoic acid. The **catalyst** is a few drops of
concentrated sulfuric acid. The **conditions** are heat. The
sulfuric acid earns its place above the arrow, not in it: a
[[catalyst]] speeds the reaction but is not consumed, so writing
it into the equation would break the atom balance — the same
bookkeeping rule that kept MnO₂ above the arrow in the
peroxide decomposition back in the rates lesson (u3:c20).

The reaction has two names, and both are examinable. It is
**[[esterification]]** — an alcohol plus a carboxylic acid
making an ester. It is also a **[[condensation-reaction]]**,
because water is produced while two molecules join together.
The condensation label is the one that matters next: the
synthetic-polymers lesson (u4:c29) builds on exactly this
join-and-expel pattern.

The third detail decides the yield. Esterification is a
[[reversible-reaction]], so the mixture sits at a position of
equilibrium (u3:c21): the position always moves to counteract
whatever change you impose. Add water to the reactants and the
position shifts left to consume it — more alcohol and acid, less
ester. That is the opposite of what you want, so the synthesis
run in reverse is guarded against: pure ethanol and pure
ethanoic acid (water-free [[glacial-ethanoic-acid]]) are used,
keeping the equilibrium stocked with reactants instead of
product-killers.

:::key-point
The concentrated sulfuric acid never enters the equation. A
catalyst is not consumed, so it appears above the arrow or not
at all — but the *conditions* line still names it, because "heat
with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid" is examinable
wording. Catalyst in the conditions, catalyst out of the
equation.
:::

:::did-you-know
Ethyl ethanoate has quite a strong smell of its own — and a day
job you have probably held in your hand. It is used as a
solvent in nail polish and nail polish remover: the same
volatility that carries fruit scents across a room also makes
it evaporate cleanly from a painted nail.
:::

:::exam-hint
State symbols in the esterification equation are all (l) — both
reactants and both products are pure liquids, not aqueous
solutions, because no water is present to dissolve them in.
That (l) is also the mark-scheme hook for the yield argument:
water is a *product*, so adding any dilutes the reactants and
pulls the equilibrium left. Pure (glacial) acid and pure
alcohol plus a drying catalyst is the recipe the mark scheme
wants.
:::

:::misconception
"Concentrated sulfuric acid is a reactant, so it belongs in the
equation." Weigh it: the acid is recovered unchanged at the end,
and the atom balance of CH₃COOH + CH₃CH₂OH already accounts for
every product atom. A catalyst changes the rate, never the
balance — into the conditions line, not into the equation.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write the esterification equation with state symbols and
the word labels under each formula? Can you name the starting
materials, the catalyst and the conditions as three separate
items? Can you explain why water must be kept out of the mixture,
using the equilibrium argument? If yes, you can make an ester on
paper — the drawing section shows you how to make any member of
the family.
:::

sections.title: Drawing and naming esters
sections.markdown:
The making section built one ester; this section builds all of
them, in both directions: formula from name, and name from
formula (4.41C), with ethyl ethanoate's own structures as the
model (4.40C).

**Building the ester.** To work out the structure of the ester
formed from any alcohol and carboxylic acid, start by drawing
the two molecules so that their –OH groups sit next to each
other. Now remove H₂O — one H and one OH — and join together
what is left. The leftover fragments bond through the ester
group, C=O joined to C–O, exactly the –COO– arrangement from
the opening section:

```
ethanol part          ethanoic-acid part
   CH₃CH₂—O—H  +  H—O—C(=O)CH₃
              ↓  −H₂O
        CH₃CH₂—O—C(=O)CH₃
           ethyl ethanoate
```

Which H and which OH are removed makes no difference to the
product: take the H from the alcohol and the OH from the acid,
or swap them, and joining the leftovers gives the same structure
either way. At International GCSE the distinction is not
examined — what is examined is the join: break the O–H pairing,
release water, bond the fragments.

An ester can be drawn either way round — CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ and
CH₃CH₂OOCCH₃ are the same molecule drawn from each end — but
the *name* is always written one way: **ethyl ethanoate**,
never "ethanoate ethyl". Keep the two drawing levels straight:
the condensed CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ is the [[structural-formula]], and
the every-bond-shown version — each C–C, C=O, C–O and O–H
drawn out — is the [[displayed-formula]]. Drawing items say
which level they want; producing the wrong level is a lost
mark even when the molecule is right.

**The naming rule.** When naming esters, the part with the C=O
is always the **'oate'** part. The name reads
[[alkyl-group]] [[alkanoate]]: the alkyl word comes from the
alcohol, the alkanoate word from the carboxylic acid. So the
'yl' bit tells you the alcohol and the 'oate' bit tells you the
carboxylic acid — **propyl butanoate** is made from propanol
and butanoic acid. Count carefully: the alkanoate carbon count
includes the carbonyl carbon, exactly as it did for the acids
(u4:c27).

**The family grid.** Three alcohols (methanol, ethanol,
propan-1-ol) crossed with three acids (methanoic, ethanoic,
propanoic) give nine esters in a three-by-three grid:

| | methanoic acid | ethanoic acid | propanoic acid |
|---|---|---|---|
| **methanol** | methyl methanoate | methyl ethanoate | methyl propanoate |
| **ethanol** | ethyl methanoate | **ethyl ethanoate** | ethyl propanoate |
| **propan-1-ol** | propyl methanoate | propyl ethanoate | propyl propanoate |

Read any cell as alcohol-row + acid-column: the row names the
alkyl part, the column names the alkanoate part. In every cell
the same trace holds: the fragment bonded through its spare
oxygen is the alcohol part, the fragment carrying the C=O is
the acid part. When each member is drawn in full with its
parents colour-coded — the alcohol parts in red, the acid
parts in blue — every bond in every one of the nine molecules
traces back to exactly one parent, which is the whole point
the grid teaches: an ester is two fragments joined through the
–COO– group, nothing more.

**Reversing the read.** You also need to work backwards: given
an ester, name the alcohol and carboxylic acid it came from.
Break the molecule apart between the single-bonded C–O inside
the ester group, then add OH to one side and H to the other so
that both fragments end with an –OH group:

CH₃COOCH₂CH₃(l) + H₂O(l) → CH₃COOH(l) + CH₃CH₂OH(l)

ethyl ethanoate + water → ethanoic acid + ethanol

The water you removed to build the ester is the water you add
back to split it. It does not actually matter which C–O bond
you break, as long as you add H to one side and OH to the other
to give two –OH groups, you will get the same answer — because
the two C–O bonds of the ester group are interchangeable under
this operation. Split ethyl ethanoate and you recover ethanol
and ethanoic acid; that is the grid cell it was born from.

:::key-point
When naming esters, the part with the C=O is always the 'oate'
part — and the name always runs alkyl-then-alkanoate. Ethyl
ethanoate: ethyl from ethanol (the alcohol), ethanoate from
ethanoic acid (the acid, carbonyl carbon counted). Methyl
propanoate: methyl from methanol, propanoate from propanoic
acid. The formula can be drawn either way round; the name
cannot.
:::

:::key-point
Splitting an ester back into its parents is insensitive to
which C–O bond you break — add H to one fragment and OH to the
other and both routes give the same two –OH molecules. Use the
bond that gives the cleaner drawing; the answer does not
change.
:::

:::worked-example
Name the ester CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ and give its parents.
*Decode:* find the ester group. The C=O carbon sits in the
CH₃CH₂C(=O)O– fragment, so the alkanoate part is propanoate —
three carbons, carbonyl included. The fragment on the other
side of the single-bonded O is CH₃–, so the alkyl part is
methyl. The ester is **methyl propanoate**. *Reverse:* split
between the C and the O of the group, add OH to the
CH₃CH₂C(=O)– side and H to the CH₃– side: **propanoic acid**
(CH₃CH₂COOH) and **methanol** (CH₃OH). Grid check: methanol
row, propanoic acid column — methyl propanoate. Consistent.
:::

:::exam-hint
The 'yl'/'oate' decode is the mark-earner in naming items: read
the name left to right, alcohol then acid. "Propyl butanoate is
made from propanol and butanoic acid" — one mark for each
parent, and the formulae must show the parents with their –OH
groups intact. When the question hands you a drawn structure
instead, locate the C=O first: the carbon bearing it starts the
alkanoate count, and everything beyond the single-bonded
oxygen is the alkyl part.
:::

:::did-you-know
Esters are often described as having a sweet, fruity smell —
and chemists have used that on purpose. Artificial flavourings
and perfumes are built by mixing esters chosen for their
scents, which is why the same family that makes nail polish
remover smell sharp also makes pear drops smell like pear.
:::

:::misconception
"Propyl butanoate comes from butanol and propanoic acid." The
words were swapped: position in the name does not track size.
The 'yl' word — propyl — names the alcohol fragment, and the
'oate' word — butanoate — names the acid fragment, regardless
of which fragment is longer. Decode left to right, alcohol
then acid, every time.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you build any grid ester by drawing the two parents with
their –OH groups adjacent and removing H₂O? Can you write
ethyl ethanoate both ways round and name it correctly? Can you
decode propyl butanoate to its parents, and split butyl
ethanoate back the other way? If yes, both directions of 4.41C
are yours.
:::

sections.title: Uses of esters
sections.markdown:
The small esters like ethyl ethanoate are commonly used as
[[solvent]]s — nail polish and nail polish remover carry them
(4.42C). But the family's headline job is scent: most esters
are used in **food flavourings and perfumes**. They are
[[volatile]] liquids — they turn to vapour easily — with
distinctive smells, and that volatility is the property doing
the work: a flavouring or perfume only works if its molecules
leave the liquid and travel through the air to your nose.

The smells are not invented; they are borrowed. The typical
smell of bananas, raspberries, pears and other fruit is due in
part to naturally occurring esters ripening inside the fruit.
Chemists create artificial flavourings and perfumes using
mixtures of esters and other organic compounds — rarely one
ester alone, because a natural fruit note is a chord, not a
single note. The lab practical coming next makes three of
these scent esters directly.

One more property separates esters from the two families that
build them, and it explains the practical's most surprising
step. Esters are hardly soluble in water, whereas small
alcohols and carboxylic acids usually are. The reason is the
–OH and –COOH groups themselves: in alcohols and acids those
groups form a special type of intermolecular force called
[[hydrogen-bond]]s with water molecules, and the attractions
between water and alcohol or acid molecules are strong enough
to pull them into solution. An ester has no O–H and no
O–H-bearing group left — its two oxygens are locked into the
–COO– arrangement — so it forms very weak interactions with
water and will not dissolve. Pour an ester into water and it
sits on top: a separate layer.

:::exam-hint
"Volatile" is a defined word, not a vibe: it means turns to
vapour easily, and it is the link between structure and use.
The full-chain answer for a uses item runs: esters are volatile
so their molecules reach the nose; they have distinctive,
often fruity smells; so they are used in food flavourings and
perfumes. Naming the use without the volatility sentence loses
the explanation mark — the property-to-use link is what the
question is testing.
:::

:::misconception
"Esters dissolve in water because they contain oxygen atoms."
Solubility in water is negotiated by O–H groups forming
hydrogen bonds with water molecules — not by oxygen atoms as
such. The ester's oxygens are buried in the –COO– group with
no hydrogen to offer, so the attractions stay weak and the
ester floats as a separate layer. Oxygen content is not the
test; hydrogen-bond capability is.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you state the two headline uses of esters and the property
that makes them work? Can you define volatile in one sentence?
Can you explain why propan-1-ol dissolves in water while
propyl ethanoate does not, in terms of hydrogen bonds? If yes,
the family's job description is clear and the practical will
feel inevitable.
:::

sections.title: Making and testing the smell of some esters in the lab
sections.markdown:
It is easy to produce esters in the lab on a test-tube scale by
reacting various combinations of carboxylic acids and alcohols
in the presence of a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid
(4.43C). The mixture has to be heated — but never by a direct
Bunsen flame, because the contents of the tubes are flammable.
A beaker of hot water at about 80 °C does the heating instead.
The full procedure for ethyl ethanoate, as run on the
test-tube scale:

1. Put 1 cm³ of ethanoic acid and 1 cm³ of ethanol into a
   boiling tube.
2. Mix well and carefully add a few drops of concentrated
   sulfuric acid.
3. Place the boiling tube in a beaker of hot water at about
   80 °C for 5 minutes.
4. Allow the contents of the tube to cool.
5. When cool, pour the mixture into a beaker half-full of
   0.5 mol/dm³ [[sodium-carbonate]] solution. There will be
   some effervescence as the excess acid reacts with the metal
   carbonate.
6. A layer of ester separates and floats on top of the water.
   The acid and alcohol mostly dissolve in the water, but the
   ester does not — the small esters float, which makes them
   easy to smell.
7. Smell the product by gently **wafting** the odour towards
   your nose with your hand. Never put your nose near the top
   of the beaker.

Two steps deserve the "why". The sodium carbonate pour exists
so that you can smell the ester better: not much ester forms in
such a short time, and the smell of the ester in the tube would
be masked by the smell of the unreacted carboxylic acid — the
carbonate mops the excess acid up (the same
carbonate-plus-acid chemistry as u2:c16, seen here as a
purification trick), and the effervescence you watch is that
mop working. The wafting step exists because the beaker holds
acid fumes and ester vapour; wafting brings a diluted sample
of the smell to your nose and keeps your face out of the
beaker.

The apparatus draws itself: a boiling tube standing in a beaker
of hot water, then the reaction mixture poured into a beaker of
cold sodium carbonate solution, where a thin layer of ester
gathers on the surface. The ester is likely to be colourless —
any colour in a drawing is there to make the layer visible, not
a property of the product.

Repeat the procedure for other combinations of acids and
alcohols. Two worth knowing by name: **butyl butanoate**, which
should smell like pineapple, and **propyl ethanoate**, which
smells like pear — run the naming decode on both and the grid
from the drawing section hands you their parents.

:::safety
Wear goggles and dispense the acids in a fume cupboard. Avoid
all skin contact with the acids; wash off immediately with
plenty of cold water if you get some on your skin. Carefully
follow the instructions as to how to smell the esters produced
— waft, never lean in.
:::

:::exam-hint
The practical item marks the *why* of each step, not just the
step. Strong answers name the hazard control (hot-water bath,
not flame — the vapours are flammable), the purification logic
(sodium carbonate removes the excess acid whose smell would
mask the ester's), and the safe-smelling technique (wafting).
A results sentence earns its mark by tying the observation to
the property: the ester floats as a separate layer because it
will not dissolve in water, and you can smell it because it is
volatile.
:::

:::misconception
"The sodium carbonate step is there to speed the reaction up."
The reaction is already over by the time the carbonate goes in
— step 5 happens after cooling. Its job is cleanup: neutralise
the leftover acid so its smell stops masking the ester's. The
effervescence is the carbonate reacting with that excess acid,
not with the ester.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you run the seven steps in order and say why the tube is
heated in a water bath rather than a flame? Can you explain the
effervescence and the reason for the sodium carbonate pour? Can
you state the safe way to smell the product? If yes, the
practical is fully loaded — repeat it mentally with other
acid–alcohol pairs: butyl butanoate should smell of pineapple,
propyl ethanoate of pear.
:::

sections.title: Chapter 28 questions
sections.markdown:
You now hold the complete [[ester]] story. The family is
defined by the –COO– functional group (4.38C); its simplest
synthesis is the [[esterification]] of ethanol with ethanoic
acid over a concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst, reversible
and therefore yield-managed (4.39C); every member can be built
from its parents and split back to them, with the
alkyl-alkanoate naming rule reading in both directions
(4.40C, 4.41C); the family's volatility and distinctive smells
make it the flavour-and-perfume workhorse (4.42C); and the
test-tube preparation — hot-water bath, carbonate cleanup,
wafted smelling — turns all of it into a procedure you can run
(4.43C). Two equations anchor the chapter: the esterification
of ethanol with ethanoic acid, and its reverse, the
water-split of [[ethyl-ethanoate]].

Every specification statement of this chapter — 4.38C to 4.43C —
has been taught, and each now joins the platform question bank
through the links below, with practice items keyed to exactly
those statements.

Before opening the bank, audit yourself against the chapter's
core moves. Can you draw –COO– and write the esterification
equation with word labels? Can you build any grid ester from
named parents and decode any ester back to them? Can you argue
the uses from volatility and the purification steps from their
chemistry? Any wobble is a section to revisit, not a reason to
start over.

The question bank for this chapter trains a predictable set of
shapes, so rehearse the moves rather than the answers. Formula
items open the set: structural formulae for named esters,
[[displayed-formula]] drawings with every bond explicit, and
naming from condensed structures — all three formula levels the
drawing section drilled. A long planning item hands you two
alcohols and two acids and asks for every ester they can make
(the grid does the counting), then the method, the detection of
the product, and two uses. Decode items run the naming rule in
reverse: named esters and drawn structures to be split back
into their alcohol and carboxylic acid parents. A synthesis
route item starts from ethanol as the only organic starting
material and builds ethyl ethanoate through it — the displayed
formula, the acid required, the oxidation that makes that acid
from ethanol (u4:c26 called back), the balanced equation and
the conditions. A closing problem hands you three unlabelled
samples — ethanol, ethanoic acid, ethyl ethanoate — and bans
smelling, so the identification must run on reactions and
physical tests you can defend. The shapes are the chapter; the
esters are just costumes.

:::exam-hint
Two habits pay in this bank. In naming and drawing items, find
the C=O first — it fixes the alkanoate word and its carbon
count, and everything beyond the single-bonded oxygen is the
alkyl word. In route items, the conditions line is worth
explicit marks: concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst named but
kept out of the equation, heat applied through a water bath,
and the yield argument (pure, water-free reagents) if the
question pushes one step further.
:::

:::misconception
"The question bank rewards memorising the answers." It rewards
the transferable routines: the C=O-first decode, the
grid build-and-split, the property-to-use argument, the
step-justified practical. The same skills re-ask through
propyl propanoate instead of ethyl ethanoate, a drawn parent
instead of a named one, a planning frame instead of an
identification frame. Run the method and the costume does not
matter.
:::

:::summary
- **The functional group (4.38C)**: esters carry –COO– — a
  carbon with C=O and C–O — the signature shared by fats, oils
  and every artificial flavouring.
- **Making ethyl ethanoate (4.39C)**:
  CH₃COOH(l) + CH₃CH₂OH(l) → CH₃COOCH₂CH₃(l) + H₂O(l) —
  esterification and condensation in one; concentrated sulfuric
  acid catalyst in the conditions, never in the equation; pure
  (glacial) reagents guard the equilibrium.
- **Drawing and naming (4.40C, 4.41C)**: draw the parents with
  –OH groups adjacent, remove H₂O, join the leftovers; name
  alkyl-then-alkanoate ('yl' from the alcohol, 'oate' from the
  acid); split any ester between the group's C and O, adding H
  and OH, to recover the parents.
- **Uses (4.42C)**: volatile liquids with distinctive smells —
  solvents (nail polish), food flavourings and perfumes; hardly
  soluble in water because no O–H remains to hydrogen-bond.
- **The practical (4.43C)**: 1 cm³ acid + 1 cm³ alcohol, few
  drops of concentrated sulfuric acid, 80 °C water bath five
  minutes, cool, pour into sodium carbonate solution, waft the
  floating ester layer — butyl butanoate (pineapple), propyl
  ethanoate (pear).
:::

:::can-you
- draw the ester functional group with both bonds explicit and
  write its condensed form?
- write the esterification equation with state symbols and word
  labels, and name the starting materials, catalyst and
  conditions as three items?
- build any of the nine grid esters from named parents and
  decode any ester back to them, both directions of the naming
  rule?
- argue the flavouring, perfume and solvent uses from
  volatility, and the floating layer from insolubility?
- run the seven-step preparation with the reason for each step,
  including the sodium carbonate pour and the wafting
  technique?
:::

:::quick-check
If every line of the Can-you checklist above is a confident
yes, you are exam-ready on 4.38C–4.43C and the platform bank
below is pure consolidation. If any line wobbled, the fix is
surgical: jump back to that section, reread the key-point box,
and redraw the structure — every section in this lesson was
built so that a single weak link can be re-forged without
redoing the family.
:::
